source: mo-tfr R2 bucket, v1/graph/graph.json (phase 1 — AI-generated synthesis, unreviewed; relational edges not yet built)

loci.label: The Eternity of God
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on parsing Boethius's formula (aeternitas est interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio) and on whether the "duration" it names truly excludes succession. Thomist (Billuart) and Jesuit (Wirceburgensis) commentators read tota simul as a single indivisible now containing every before and after without division [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-1/p229]; the Scotist Frassen instead glosses vitae, following Scotus's Quodlibet VI, as vicariously standing for the whole array of essential and attributive perfections [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p332]. Lutheran systematics (Calov, Gerhard, Olearius, Buddeus, Quenstedt) fold the same tota-simul doctrine into a cross-confessional consensus reaching Reformed (Sedan Academy) and Catholic (Aguirre) authors, tying eternity to simplicity and immutability [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-2/p404]. A live dispute concerns eternity's formal reason: Calov, invoking the Jesuit metaphysician Hurtado de Mendoza, weighs bare interminability of being against permanence taken "eminently" [calov-scripta-philosophica/p386]. The chief heterodox challenge comes from the Socinian Crellius, who reads Scripture's "was/is/will be" and "age to age" as implying real succession in God's duration, which Calov rejects as accommodated speech [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-2/p449].

loci.label: Angels
loci.ov: In this corpus the treatise de angelis turns less on whether angels exist — dispatched briskly from Scripture and reason in nearly every loci-theologici treatment — than on how a purely spiritual creature knows, and what is owed to it in worship. Reformed and Lutheran loci-theologici (Calov, opening the locus under Nomina [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-4/p81]; Chemnitz, Heidegger, Olearius, Hollaz, Marck, Voetius) catalogue names and office before nature, then close by denying angels any right to invocation, reserved to God and the Mediator alone [martini-christiana-et-catholica-fides/p163] — the confessional line separating them from the Catholic commentary tradition dominating engagement here: Jesuits (Suárez, Vásquez, Becanus), Thomists (de Soto/Zumel, Sylvius, Poinsot, Gonet, Billuart), Scotists (Frassen, Scotus Academicus), and the older Bonaventurian-Franciscan line (Barberi ad mentem S. Bonaventurae, and Bonaventure's own Sentences commentary), who divide chiefly over angelic individuation and cognition. Posewitz's Lutheran scholasticism weighs syllogistically whether angels know all things outside God, and denies it [johann-heinrich-posewitz-theologia-scholastica/p631]; Billuart's Thomist commentary grounds angel-to-angel knowledge in species infused at creation, per Augustine [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-3/p422]. Even the matutinal/vespertinal distinction organizing this cognition debate is flagged by the Reformed Voetius himself as a later scholastic gloss on Augustine, traced to Alexander of Hales and Bonaventure rather than Augustine's own idiom [voetius-selectae-disputationes-theologicae-vol-5/p276].

loci.label: The Divine Attributes & their Distinction
loci.ov: Given absolute divine simplicity, the question this sub-locus turns on is how the attributes are distinguished — from the essence and from one another — without multiplying beings in God or collapsing them into bare synonyms. The extremes are old: Eunomius denied any distinction at all, and the debate already had a medieval controversy over whether "divinity" differs from "God," condemned at Reims 1148 [tournely-praelectiones-theologicae-vol-1/p180]. Among this corpus's Baroque scholastics, Thomist manualists (Billuart, Zigliara) hold real identity with the essence, admitting only a distinction of reason "with foundation in the thing" — the virtual distinction — since one infinite perfection grounds really-diverse created effects [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-1/p146]; the Salamanca Thomists press this to intellect and will specifically, distinguished ex natura rei as principles of the real trinitarian processions [domingo-de-soto-zumel-salamanca-commentary-vol-1/p788]. Scotists (Mastri, Frassen, Bonaventura Baro) instead hold Scotus's own formal distinction a parte rei; Lafosse, doxographizing carefully, separates this from Gregory of Rimini's reduction of the same question to a distinction of reason, warning against flattening Scotus's own view into bare virtual-distinction-plus-eminence [fulgentius-lafosse-augustinus-theologus-sive-theologia-secundum-genium-2/p220]. Reformed (Alting, Baron) and Lutheran (Scheibler) scholastics converge on the moderate line, invoking the scholastic commonplace dividing reason's distinction into "reasoning" and "reasoned" varieties [robert-baron-of-st-andrews-metaphysica-generalis-as/p393].

loci.label: Baptism
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on two entangled questions: whether baptism is the instrumental cause of regeneration or only its sign and seal, and whether its necessity is absolute or merely "ordinate." Reformed writers (Scharp, explicitly refuting Bellarmine and Trent, together with Heidegger, Daneau, and Vitringa) deny causal efficacy, holding baptism a moral means and sign of the covenant rather than its cause; necessity binds by precept, not as a means to salvation, so infants dying unbaptized without contempt of the sacrament are not thereby lost [scharp-cursus-theologicus/p652]. The Catholic Sentences-tradition (Estius) holds the harder Tridentine line: baptism strictly necessary and causally efficacious even for infants, against a taxonomy of Anabaptist errors he lays out [estius-in-quatuor-libros-sententiarum-commentaria-liber-iv-pars-i/p121]. Lutherans (Gerhard, Calov, Buddeus, Dannhauer, Melanchthon) hold a middle position — baptism really regenerates infants as an ordinarily, not absolutely, necessary means — defended against Socinian sacrament-denial via the circumcision-baptism typology [calov-socinismus-profligatus/p878] and against the Reformed denial of infant efficacy [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-4/p1043]. Across all three camps, paedobaptism rests on the covenant-inclusion of believers' children, against the Anabaptists [maccovius-loci-communes-collegia-theologica-vol-1/p940].

loci.label: Christ / Christology
loci.ov: The corpus's Christological center of gravity is the hypostatic union — how two complete, distinct natures subsist in one person of the Word [chemnitz-de-duabus-naturis-in-christo/p81] — and its corollary, the communicatio idiomatum. Chemnitz already grades that communication into degrees [chemnitz-de-duabus-naturis-in-christo/p190], the seed that later Lutheran orthodoxy (Hollaz, Olearius, Calov, Quenstedt) formalizes into named genera, including a real, non-local (repletive) presence of Christ's exalted humanity. Reformed authors affirm the same personal union but reject that inference: Heidanus confines communicatio to three narrow senses in which the Word communicates hypostasis to the flesh [heidanus-corpus-theologiae-christianae/p113], and Matthias Martini calls the leap to omnipresent flesh a perversion of the union's mystery [martini-christiana-et-catholica-fides/p272] — though Fabricius (ed. Heidegger) shows Daneau conceding to Chemnitz on the narrower point that the Logos was already a hypostasis before the union. Catholic scholastics ground the same dogma in conciliar authority, against Nestorius at Ephesus [wirceburgensis-theologia-wirceburgensis-vol-2/p682], while the Thomist Salamanticenses and the Scotist Frassen carry Bonaventure's question from the Sentences — whether Christ's humanity keeps its own act of existence — forward into the era of Suárez.

loci.label: The Lord's Supper
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus is organized around Trent's transubstantiation as the shared foil. Catholic/Jesuit-Thomist manuals (Suárez, Vásquez, the Salamanticenses, Becanus, Tournely, Wirceburgensis) elaborate the conciliar definition of substantial conversion; Reformed polemic answers by title alone — Heidegger's Tumulus Concilii Tridentini, Chamier's Panstratia Catholica. Lutheran orthodoxy reads the verba institutionis literally and asserts a true, real, substantial presence of Christ's body and blood (Gerhard, Loci V, "de vera reali & substantiali...praesentia" [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-5/p213]), grounding it in the personal union of Logos and flesh against the "modos praesentiae Calvinianos" [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-9/p356] — yet, in careful hands, denying both transubstantiation and any local, durable affixing of body to bread outside use [johann-fabricius-consideratio-controversiarum/p181]. Reformed orthodoxy instead holds a real but strictly spiritual presence, given to faith by the Spirit and set against corporal or merely symbolic modes [heidegger-corpus-theologiae-christianae-vol-3/p466], pressing the "memorial" and "until he come" texts toward the conclusion that Christ's body is not corporally present now [pareus-collegia-theologica/p408]. The fault line throughout is not whether Christ is truly given, but whether substantially, spiritually, or commemoratively.

loci.label: Creation
loci.ov: Every school glosses one formula, creatio est productio rei ex nihilo, but the corpus's status quaestionis turns on three linked questions. First, what "nothing" and "from" mean: seventeenth-century Lutheran and Reformed scholastics inherit and refine the distinction of nihil negativum from privativum and read "ex" as denoting a term-from-which rather than a material cause [johann-heinrich-posewitz-theologia-scholastica/p478]. Second, whether the world could have been created ab aeterno: Reformed authors such as Burgersdijck rule this out as self-contradictory, since non-being must precede the thing in time [burgersdijck-metaphysica-as/p300], whereas Cornelius a Lapide instead distinguishes a licit "creating in eternity" from an incoherent "creating at eternity's beginning" [cornelius-a-lapide-commentaria-in-sacram-scripturam-vol-1/p101]. Third, the shared front against matter-eternalism: Daneau's polemic against Hermogenian and Stoic coeternal matter, invoking Justin Martyr's ποιητής/δημιουργός contrast [daneau-christianae-isagoges/p90], runs parallel to Calov's rejection of Maccovius's claim that creation is really identical with God's own essence [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-3/p938]. Suárez, the Salamanca Thomists (Soto/Zumel), and Rada's running Thomist-Scotist controversies work these same questions from the Catholic side, while Voetius's circle presses a further, more technical dispute over whether material forms are created independently of their matter.

loci.label: God
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus De Deo turns less on God's bare existence (presupposed via Exod. 3:14, cited repeatedly as "Ego sum qui sum") than on how the divine attributes can be classified without compromising simplicity. Reformed scholastics — Crocius, Leydekker, the Sedan Academy's Thesaurus — treat simplicity as the paradigmatic attribute of the divine essence, sorting the whole class into negative/affirmative, or "incommunicable" (essence: primacy, simplicity, infinity) versus "communicable" (life: wisdom, goodness), reached via the triplex via of negation, causality, and eminence [leydekker-medulla-theologica/p50]. Voetius works the same terrain through the Scholastic-Metaphysician tradition, distinguishing merely comparative from absolutely supreme simplicity [voetius-selectae-disputationes-theologicae-vol-1/p280]. Lutheran dogmaticians (Hollaz, Baier, Calov) run a parallel apparatus, but Gerhard grounds simplicity patristically, borrowing Augustine's De Trinitate argument that the soul's manifold faculties prove only God is truly simple [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1/p280]. Petavius argues the same conclusion historically from Greek patristic testimony rather than syllogism [petavius-de-theologicis-dogmatibus-vol-1/p254], while Frassen's Scotus Academicus presses how such simplicity coheres with the really distinct divine persons [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p293] — and the corpus's other most-engaged works here, the Thomist Soto/Zumel commentary on the Summa and Suárez's Opera, attest the same essence/attribute problem organizing De Deo across confessions.

loci.label: The Church
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus de ecclesia turns on two linked questions: what the Church essentially is, and by what marks the true visible Church is known. Reformed and Lutheran authors converge on distinguishing an invisible Church of the elect, known to God through internal faith and charity, from the Church as visible society, gathered by professed word and administered sacrament [gerhard-confessio-catholica-liber-2-pars-1/p1172]. Both traditions narrow the notae ecclesiae toward that word-and-sacrament core, discarding Bellarmine's fuller Catholic list — antiquity, succession, miracles, temporal felicity — as no true marks at all [martini-methodus-theologiae/p182], and Alsted works the same ground as an essential/accidental distinction, with discipline demoted to an accidental note [alsted-theologia-scholastica-didactica/p626]. Against the charge that this leaves the Church intermittently invisible, Gerhard argues it can shrink to a hidden remnant without ceasing to be the true Church [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-5/p777], whereas Habert holds flatly that the true Church, wanting no sensible mark, is always visible [habert-theologia-dogmatica-moralis-vol-1/p186]. A second axis, governance, sets Suárez's papal-hierarchical Opera against Voetius's presbyterial Politica Ecclesiastica, Carpzov's Lutheran territorial-consistorial Isagoge, and Chamier's standing anti-Roman Panstratia.

loci.label: The Gospel
loci.ov: What "Gospel" properly names, and how it relates to the Law, is the operative question here. Authors work from Melanchthon's founding antithesis -- Moses' curse against Christ's free forgiveness, glossing John 1:17's grace and truth against law [philipp-melanchthon-opera-vol-22/p177] -- through Chemnitz's etymological grounding of "Law and Promise" [chemnitz-loci-theologici-pars-2/p581], to later Lutheran orthodoxy's systematized differentiae legis et evangelii: Gospel as doctrina fidei against Law's doctrina operum, its promises gratuitous rather than compensatory (Hollaz) [david-hollaz-examen-theologicum-acroamaticum/p1069]. Gerhard sharpens this into a broad sense (the whole scriptural doctrine, Old Testament and New) against a strict, proper sense -- "the most joyful proclamation" of gratuitous remission in Christ [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-3/p492]. Reformed authors take a different tack toward continuity: Voetius holds the covenant one in essence across the Old and New Testaments, differing only in "mode and circumstances of dispensation" [voetius-selectae-disputationes-theologicae-vol-4/p29] -- the continuity that Coccejus's federal theology, this topic's most-engaged author, builds into a single unfolding covenant of grace. Viret and Piscator engage the Gospel more as preaching and commentary than taxonomy; Catholic exegesis (a Lapide) works outside this Protestant scholastic grid.

loci.label: The Existence of God
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on the scholastic quaestio an existentia Dei demonstrari possit: is God's existence self-evident, or must it be demonstrated, and if demonstrated, a priori or only a posteriori? Catholic manuals converge, Jesuit and Thomist alike: not self-evident quoad nos, and undemonstrable a priori since God has no cause of Himself, so demonstratio a posteriori/quia from effects (Aquinas's five ways) is the sole legitimate route — thus Wirceburgensis [wirceburgensis-theologia-wirceburgensis-vol-2/p20], hedging on whether Anselm himself meant strict demonstration, and Billuart [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-1/p68], distinguishing demonstratio propter quid from quia; Sylvester of Ferrara's Contra Gentiles commentary and the Salamanca Soto-Zumel line continue the same Thomist proof-tradition, while Aguirre's Theologia S. Anselmi (De Deo Uno) reworks Anselm's own case. Protestant scholastics run parallel apparatus: Lutheran Schulmetaphysik (Jakob Martini [jakob-martini-exercitationes-metaphysicae/p624]) sorts logical/metaphysical/physical proofs, citing Damascene's innate cognitio Dei; among the Reformed, Voetius's Utrecht orthodoxy opposes Cartesian rationalism, while Braun [braun-doctrina-foederum/p82] instead redeploys the idea of a most-perfect being as itself an a posteriori proof. The "a priori/a simultaneo" label later given this Anselm-Descartes-Leibniz line [tommaso-zigliara-summa-philosophica-vol-2/p384] is a nineteenth-century neo-Thomist systematization, not early-modern usage.

loci.label: Faith
loci.ov: Across this corpus de fide converges on one contested question: does the essence of justifying faith lie in assensus, intellectual assent to revealed truths on God's authority, or in fiducia, a special trust that Christ's benefits and the remission of sins are given to oneself? Catholic controversialists Piggius and Tapper, answered by the Lutheran Gerhard, call the Protestant fiducial account a "monster and chimera" conflating intellect and will, with no scriptural warrant for such personal certainty [gerhard-confessio-catholica-liber-2-pars-3/p667]. Trent's Canon 12, invoked by the Thomist Billuart, confines faith to assent on divine authority and reassigns fiducia to hope, spes roborata [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-6/p455]. Reformed and Lutheran orthodoxy answer that bare assent, had even by devils, cannot be justifying faith: Pareus makes fiducia the differentia turning generic faith into the species fides justificans [pareus-de-gratia-de-iustificatione-2/p261]. The line is not simply confessional: the Reformed Heidegger enlists the pre-Tridentine Cardinal Contarini, who had joined assent and trust inseparably, against Trent's own later hardening [heidegger-tumulus-concilii-tridentini-vol-1/p468], while Arminius, per Hoornbeek, denies that assurance of one's own forgiveness constitutes faith rather than following upon justification [hoornbeek-theologiae-practicae/p790].

loci.label: The Filioque & the Procession of the Spirit
loci.ov: In this corpus the dispute is not whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as the Father — Thomists (Soto/Zumel, Salamanticenses), the Catholic Zamora, Lutherans (Gerhard, Calov, Posewitz), the Reformed Hyperius, and the Scotist Frassen all affirm this against the Greeks — but how to state the manner of procession without positing two principles or two spirations. The common formula, which Gerhard traces to the Second Council of Lyons, holds that Father and Son spirate "not as from two principles... but as from one principle, not by two spirations, but by a single spiration" [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1/p680]. Salamanticenses, following Aquinas, presses this to deny any priority whatever between Father and Son as spirators [salamanticenses-cursus-theologicus-vol-3/p620], whereas Zamora reports Scotus and Gabriel Biel disagreeing over whether even a loose "order of origin" between them remains speakable [zamora-disputationes-theologicae-de-deo-uno-et-trino/p2148]. A separate, more polemical question — whether Rome's unilateral creedal addition was licit — occupies Frassen's account of the Photian schism [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-3/p245], while Posewitz argues against the Catholic van Walenburch brothers that the doctrine needs no unwritten tradition, being provable from Scripture's own sense [johann-heinrich-posewitz-theologia-scholastica/p218].

loci.label: Covenant
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on three linked questions: whether Scripture teaches two covenants, of works and of grace, or a third distinct Mosaic pact; whether the foedus gratiae is conditional or absolute; and whether the Old and New Testament administrations are one covenant or two. The bipartite schema, anatomized into stipulatio/promissio/adstipulatio/restipulatio, is the signature of the Cocceian federal school: Cocceius himself defines the berith as a mutual pact of peace and friendship [coccejus-summa-theologiae/p435], and the Cocceian Johannes Braun systematizes it, following Cameron in refusing a third "Mosaic" covenant as merely a new economy of the one covenant of grace [braun-doctrina-foederum/p281]. Scharp's earlier Reformed scholasticism reaches a similar one-covenant-two-administrations verdict from the Pauline letter/spirit contrast (ministration of death vs. life, veil removed) [scharp-cursus-theologicus/p344], independent of Cocceian pact-language. The sharper fault line is conditionality: against Antinomian claims of a wholly absolute covenant, Mastricht distinguishes means-promises (absolute) from end-promises, conditional on faith rather than free will [mastricht-theoretico-practica-theologia/p535] — a line Vitringa's later excursus traces through Lutheran orthodoxy (Gerhard, Hülsemann) as consensus with the Reformed against Bellarmine and the Socinian Volkelius, both of whom make the covenant's condition operative righteousness, not faith [vitringa-sr-observationes-sacrae-vol-4/p239].

loci.label: Grace
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus de gratia turns almost entirely on the question bequeathed by the Congregatio de Auxiliis: does grace's efficacy consist in an intrinsic divine determination of the will prior to its act, or in the will's free consent to a grace already sufficient in itself? Thomists (Salamanticenses, Poinsot, Gonet, Billuart) locate efficacy in a causal auxilium efficax/praemotio physica antecedent to the will's own operation [salamanticenses-cursus-theologicus-vol-10/p232], against Jesuits (Suárez, Ripalda, Becanus), who as Molinists or Congruists ground it in the will's consent or in a divinely-foreseen congruous occasion (scientia media) — a tripartite schema (Molinist/Congruist/Thomist) that itself crystallizes only in the later manual tradition [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-6/p362]. Jansenius radicalizes Augustine against every congruist mediation, denying that Christ's medicinal grace retains sufficient grace's essential "indifference" to use and neglect [jansenius-augustinus/p962]. The same efficax/sufficiens vocabulary crosses confessional lines: Hülsemann's Lutheran De Auxiliis Gratiae argues for an intrinsically efficacious yet resistible grace [hulsemann-de-auxiliis-gratiae/p335], while Testard's Reformed Eirenikon recasts it as general (universally offered) versus particular (efficaciously applied to the elect) grace [paul-testard-eirenikon-seu-synopsis-doctrinae-de-natura-et-gratia-bloi/p273].

loci.label: Man / Anthropology
loci.ov: The de-homine locus in this corpus turns above all on the imago Dei — where it resides and what it consists in — set within the wider frame of man's body-soul composition and his state before and after the fall (Aguirre's De Natura Hominis Pura et Lapsa; Meisner's dedicated Anthropologia Sacra). Lutheran orthodoxy makes the image an accidental, concreated perfection distinct from the soul's own faculties: Baier, invoking Dannhauer and Luther's gloss on Genesis, insists memory, will and mind survive the fall precisely because it is the image, not the faculties, that is lost [baier-compendium-theologiae-positivae-vol-2/p149]. Reformed authors split: Spanheim rejects the Scholastic reading of Augustine's mental triad as a "mirror of the Trinity," referring the image to the essence common to the persons rather than to the persons as such [spanheim-disputationum-miscellanearum/p121], while Vitringa reports Coccejus confining it to moral rectitude against Leydekker's broader inclusion of the soul's spirituality, faculties, and immortality [vitringa-sr-observationes-sacrae-vol-2/p166]. Catholic manuals formalize a twofold natural/supernatural image (Habert, quoting Augustine's "intus, non in corpore") [habert-theologia-dogmatica-moralis-vol-1/p824], while the Scotist Frassen recasts the same triad as a dispute over whether the soul's powers are really distinct [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-5/p158].

loci.label: Divine Omnipresence & Immensity
loci.ov: The question in this corpus is less whether God is omnipresent than how immensity is conceived without composition or place, and whether it is even the same notion as omnipresence or ubiquity. Bradwardine, bypassing the scholastic ubi-grammar, reaches for the pseudo-Hermetic "infinite sphere whose center is everywhere, circumference nowhere" [thomas-bradwardine-thomas-bradwardine-de-causa-dei/p189]; Reformed writers like Snecanus and Ludwig Crocius still favor the older essence-presence-power grammar and the "whole in the whole" formula over any tripartite schema. The circumscriptive/definitive/repletive taxonomy, medieval in origin, is deployed with fresh fluency in Baroque scholasticism: the Sorbonne's Tournely wields it while cataloguing errors from Jews who confined God to the Temple to Platonists who housed him in a fiery sphere [tournely-praelectiones-theologicae-vol-1/p224], while the Scotist Frassen instead distinguishes Presence, Ubiquity, and Immensity as three formally separate notions, with a graded fourfold "dwelling" of God in creatures [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p308]. The Reformed scholastic Keckermann rejects "repletively" as an improper term, since God is strictly contained nowhere [keckermann-systema-ss-theologiae/p105]; Lutheran Calov, by contrast, distinguishes immensity (essential, absolute) from omnipresence (external, relative, operative) [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-2/p399] — a distinction with stakes for the Christological ubiquity dispute that Wendelin's Contra Gerhardum, on this same shelf, is aimed against.

loci.label: Justification
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on one question: is justifying righteousness IMPUTED — Christ's righteousness reckoned to the believer through faith — or INFUSED, a created habit of grace and charity making the sinner formally, intrinsically righteous? Trent's Acta and its scholastic defenders (Vega's De Iustificatione, Suárez, the Thomist Salamanticenses, the Walenburg brothers) hold the latter, requiring infused charity and congruent or condign merit alongside faith. Becanus's Manuale states the Protestant alternative precisely in order to refute it: an alien righteousness leaving the believer "in himself a sinner... only held to be righteous... on account of another's righteousness imputed to him" [becanus-manuale-controversiarum/p421]. Against Rome, Lutheran and Reformed writers converge. Melanchthon's Apology grounds sola fide in reconciliation "on account of Christ" [melanchthon-confessio-augustana-apologia/p175]; Calov invokes the Formula of Concord's rule that faith justifies not as a meritorious work but as the instrument apprehending an alien righteousness [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-10/p223]; Pareus states flatly that "our righteousness is not inherent, but imputed" [pareus-de-gratia-de-iustificatione-2/p609]. A further front runs within Reformed orthodoxy: Vitringa turns the same formula against Remonstrants who make faith's own act, not Christ's righteousness, the thing reckoned [vitringa-sr-observationes-sacrae-vol-3/p300] — a fracture Chamier, Voetius, Coccejus, and Heidegger's anti-Tridentine Tumulus all presuppose.

loci.label: The Law
loci.ov: Across this corpus the locus divides law into moral (republished natural law), ceremonial, and judicial/forensic — a distinction already implicit in Aquinas's reading of the Decalogue but hardened into a fixed technical scheme by the Reformed and Lutheran scholastics engaged here. The live question is what "abrogation" means: nearly every author agrees ceremonial and judicial law lapse at Christ's advent, but the moral law is abrogated only as to its curse and coercive power, not its doctrine or claim on obedience [pareus-collegia-theologica/485]; Chemnitz makes the point grammatically — Paul's "dead to the law" describes believers, not an inoperative law itself [chemnitz-loci-theologici-pars-2/79]. Reformed authors elaborate a doctrine of the law's twofold use, common to elect and reprobate alike and proper to the regenerate [polanus-amandus-polanus-syntagma-theologiae-christianae-liber-vi-de-pr/32]. Catholic scholastics (Becanus, following Aquinas Ia-IIae and Soto/Driedo) retain a broader treatise-of-law framework rather than this Protestant tripartite division [becanus-summa-theologiae-scholasticae-pars-2/447], while Suárez supplies the era's most systematic natural-law philosophy. Within Reformed orthodoxy, Coccejus's federal covenant theology and Voetius's precisionism mark the sharpest internal fault line, chiefly over the Sabbath's continuing obligation. Selden's rabbinic, Noahide approach — natural law binding all nations, distinct from Israel's ceremonial and judicial law — stands outside every scholastic taxonomy here [selden-de-jure-naturali-et-gentium/85].

loci.label: Free Will
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on two linked questions. First, does fallen liberum arbitrium retain a real indifference to good and evil, or only a captivity from which grace alone liberates it — patristic testimony assembled by Jansenist compilers frames the will as free only toward evil unless freed by gift [leydekker-de-historia-jansenismi/p492]. Second, granting some liberty survives, how is its exercise reconciled with efficacious grace and predestination? Molina's Concordia grounds this in scientia media, God's foreknowledge of what a self-determining will would freely do under any concourse [molina-concordia-liberi-arbitrii-vol-1/p370]; Suárez and Bellarmine extend the position, but the Thomist Salamanticenses dismiss it as multiplying arbitrary "middle knowledges" [salamanticenses-cursus-theologicus-vol-10/p58], while Jansenius instead relocates all liberty into one formal ratio libertatis, shared but differently determined by God, the blessed, and the damned [jansenius-augustinus/p1195]. Voetius joins the Thomists against Molinist "indifferent concursus" as explanatorily empty [voetius-selectae-disputationes-theologicae-vol-1/p384], even as Reformed and Lutheran authors (Chamier, Holzfuß, Meisner) stand with Luther's bondage-of-the-will against Rome as such. Bonaventure and Driedo work the same Augustinian material before this de-auxiliis apparatus existed.

loci.label: Christian Liberty
loci.ov: The corpus organizes this locus around three linked questions: from what does Christ's liberation actually free the believer; where does that freedom's boundary fall; and who governs conscience in what it leaves untouched. Reformed and Lutheran scholastics substantially converge: Junius defines liberty as the faithful's "gratuitous and spiritual manumission" from the law's curse, sin's slavery, and the yoke of ceremonies and adiaphora [franciscus-junius-opera-theologica-vol-1/p1101], and Olearius's Lutheran Universa Theologia sets out nearly the same four-part scheme — a scholastic systematization of Luther's blunter 1520 paradox (lord of all, servant of all). Alsted names the boundary precisely: liberty's proper object is the ceremonial law, the civil/forensic law only in part [alsted-theologia-scholastica-didactica/p784]. The sharpest confessional line runs over church power: Pareus mounts a two-front defense, rebutting Bellarmine's charge that Reformed liberty voids all law and the Anabaptists' actual use of that same liberty to shed civil obedience [pareus-collegia-theologica/p863], while Heidegger's anti-Tridentine polemic denies ecclesiastical statute any claim on a conscience answerable to God alone [heidegger-tumulus-tridentini-concilii/p730]. Bullinger's paradox binds both fronts: true Christian liberty is a perpetual servitude by which we serve God [bullinger-decades/p468]. Driedo's Catholic De Libertate Christiana, written against Luther, locates liberty within ecclesiastical precept rather than against it.

loci.label: The Civil Magistrate
loci.ov: The literature here turns on one formula, posed most sharply by the high-orthodox systematics as an Magistratus Politicus potestatem habeat circa sacra [bechmann-theologia-polemica/p1078] — how far civil rule reaches into religion, short of the ministry's own preaching, sacraments, and power of the keys. Gerhard's Confessio Catholica states the Lutheran territorial-church thesis that the Christian magistrate cannot be excluded from cura sacrorum and judgment of religious controversies [gerhard-confessio-catholica-liber-2-pars-2/p454]. Beza's earlier, harder Genevan position makes the magistrate Dei vicarius, bound first to establish and guard true worship, then to frame just civil law — grounds enough to justify coercing heretics [beza-de-haereticis-puniendis/p26]; this vicarius-idiom predates the crisper circa sacra apparatus of the later scholastics. The later Reformed line (Daneau, Marck, Voetius) relocates the boundary to the mode of coercion — civil-corporal penalty versus ecclesiastical censure alone — and Voetius, invoking the conformist bishop Davenant, trichotomizes instruction, spiritual coercion, and external coercion [voetius-politica-ecclesiastica-vol-1/p188]. Hülsemann even reports Reformed-on-Reformed disagreement over reach, the Leiden theologians wanting coercion extended into private religious practice [hulsemann-extensio-breviarii-theologici/p440].

loci.label: Last Things
loci.ov: In this corpus de novissimis is contested on four fronts: how the topic itself is enumerated, the identity of the risen body, the nature of the judgment(s), and the state of the soul between death and resurrection. Systematic loci-writers (Gerhard, Heidanus, Vossius, Polanus) organize the matter variously; Gerhard notes that Bernard's older mnemonic of four novissima (death, judgment, hell, glory) omits the resurrection and the world's end, and substitutes his own sixfold scheme [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-8/18] — the fourfold tag is a medieval homiletic inheritance, not fixed dogma. Vossius, following the scholastic Durandus, distinguishes a secret particular judgment at death from the public universal judgment on the last day [vossius-theses-theologicae/239]. Pareus insists on the raised body's numerical identity against Sadducees, the Hymenaeus-Philetus line, and Anabaptists who imagine wholly new bodies [pareus-collegia-theologica/457], while Calov's anti-Socinian polemic distinguishes the separated soul's immediate beatitude after death from its consummation, deferred to the resurrection [calov-socinismus-profligatus/1082]. The corpus's heaviest engagement with the locus, though, runs through the Trent controversy over purgatory and suffrages for the dead: Bellarmine and Suárez uphold the Tridentine position against Chemnitz's Examen, Heidegger's Tumulus Concilii Tridentini, Crocius's Anti-Becanus, and Chamier's Panstratia — the sharpest confessional line here.

loci.label: Prayer
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus bifurcates. Catholic scholastics ask what kind of act prayer is and how it causes its effect — the single most-consulted text here is Suárez's own quaestio, which, siding with Scotus, denies that ordinatio belongs to the intellect (against Thomas and the Thomists) and defines prayer as a will-borne desiderium completed only when intellect renders it locutio to God, purely mental prayer to God being reducible to an act of the will [suarez-opera-vol-14/p33]. Habert's moral theology specifies the conditions of a valid petition — awareness of need, desire, hope, a hearer who perceives — reading the bare act of asking as Augustine's proof against the Pelagians that grace is necessary [habert-theologia-dogmatica-moralis-vol-8/p486]; the later Wirceburgensis manual then worries how petition moves God without a physical, efficient causality incompatible with immutability, resolving impetration into a moral cause exercised only "by way of supplication" [wirceburgensis-theologia-wirceburgensis-vol-3/p877]. Reformed orthodoxy (Bucanus, Pictet, Voetius, Coccejus, Rivet) and Lutheran orthodoxy (Melanchthon, Carpzov) instead catechize the locus by ends and fruits rather than causal mechanics — Bucanus's twofold end, God's glory and our utility [bucanus-institutiones-theologicae-1602/p408], Melanchthon's petition-and-thanksgiving pressed against doubt [philipp-melanchthon-opera-vol-23/p53] — testing prayer by sincerity of faith rather than scholastic analysis of its causality.

loci.label: Sin
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns less on sin's genus -- Augustine's Contra Faustum formula (factum, vel dictum, vel concupitum contra legem aeternam) and the originale/actuale division are shared scholastic property across Jesuit, Lutheran, and Reformed authors alike [becanus-summa-theologiae-scholasticae-pars-2/p258] -- than on original sin's formal cause, the question that draws the corpus's heaviest engagement (Suárez, Vásquez, Salamanticenses, Becanus, Bonaventure). Gerhard glosses original sin as privatio boni, corruption without subsistence, citing Bonaventure's Compendium for the same division [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-2/p710]. Heidegger's own doxography then sorts the medieval inheritance into Thomists-with-Augustine (concupiscence as the positive element) against Scotists-with-Anselm (bare carentia of original justice), names Bellarmine's privation-of-a-supernatural-gift as the common Roman view, and notes even Soto rejected Catharinus/Pighius's reduction to mere imputation [heidegger-corpus-theologiae-christianae-vol-3/p169]. Reformed writers sit at neither pole: Pareus presses whether Bellarmine's bare privation is sin at all apart from the law that condemns it, elsewhere defining original sin as privation of the mind's rectitude toward God plus a positive inclination against his law -- nature's own wound, not a forfeited supernatural extra [pareus-de-gratia-de-iustificatione/p976; pareus-collegia-theologica/p216].

loci.label: Omnipotence & Absolute Power
loci.ov: The locus turns on whether God's power divides really or only rationally into potentia absoluta — what implies no contradiction, considered per se apart from intellect and will — and potentia ordinata — what accords with his actual decree — and whether the distinction is ever more than notional. Aquinas's own formula anchors the debate [de-potentia-dei-cum-commentariis/p95]. Thomists (Capreolus, Soto/Zumel, the Salamanticenses, John of St. Thomas) elaborate it: John of St. Thomas, noting that Aquinas and Scotus alike recognized only the ordinata/absoluta pair, presses past the moderns' habit of treating ordinata and ordinaria as synonyms to distinguish the two according to diverse respects [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-3-pt-2/p422]. Jesuits (Suárez, Ripalda) work the same question from Fonseca's charge that on the standard reading nothing is ever actually done by potentia absoluta — a critique Reformed metaphysician Robert Baron also relays [robert-baron-of-st-andrews-metaphysica-generalis/p119]. Reformed precisianists (Voetius, Alsted, Chamier) press adjacent questions — Maccovius denies God any passive potentia whatsoever [maccovius-loci-communes-collegia-theologica-vol-1/p667] — while Lutherans (Calov, Carpzov) converge with Scheibler, who reduces the plurality to inadequate concepts of one simple power [christoph-scheibler-metaphysica-duobus-libris-geneva-1636-protestant-s/p647], on a rational rather than real distinction. Snecanus, earlier, states the absolute/actual pairing by scriptural accumulation alone, without this apparatus.

loci.label: Predestination
loci.ov: Across this corpus the locus turns on one question: does God's eternal decree to save some and pass by others rest on his bare good pleasure, or does it also look to something foreseen — faith, merit, sin? Reformed orthodoxy answers absolutely: election is grounded not on account of their foreseen faith, piety, or good works [pareus-collegia-theologica/p234]. Davenant's Dissertatio presses the same logic onto reprobation: taking up Bellarmine's language of preterition as the negative act of reprobation, he insists — against a Scotist-leaning reading — that this negation still contains an expressed, affirmed divine will [davenant-dissertatio-de-praedestinatione-et-reprobatione/p8]. Martini nonetheless locates the decree's occasion in the foreknown Fall (the infralapsarian construal), and Amyraut's Saumur school keeps election unconditional while relocating universality in hypothetical grace. Lutherans break the symmetry: Scherzer grounds reprobation in those God foresaw would finally reject offered grace [johann-adam-scherzer-systema-theologiae/p503], restricting predestination proper to the elect. Catholics split internally: Thomists like Poinsot hold election to glory prior to election to grace, so that negative reprobation — exclusion from glory — rests on God's sheer will before any foreseen sin, only the punitive act presupposing it [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-3-pt-2/p334], while Suárez's congruism likewise roots non-election in the divine will, resisting any grounding of the choice itself in foreseen merit [suarez-opera-vol-11/p141].

loci.label: The Divine Processions & Eternal Generation
loci.ov: This locus turns on why the Son's generation and the Spirit's procession must be really distinct productions, and what principle secures the distinction. Building on Augustine's verbum/amor analogy and Anselm's contrast of nasci and donum [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p255], the Latin schools ground the difference in intellect versus will: the Word proceeds as an assimilative conception bearing the Father's likeness, properly "generation" [wirceburgensis-theologia-wirceburgensis-vol-2/p410], while the Spirit proceeds as love, a union rather than an assimilation, hence "procession" simply. Frassen reports this as the view of "almost all the Thomists" - the same architecture organizes the Trinitarian tracts of Gonet, Poinsot, and Billuart - then presses the Scotist objection that intellectual likeness is merely intentional, not natural, and so cannot alone found true generation [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-3/p129]. Reformed scholastics like Polanus work the same ground through Damascene's Greek gennetos/ekporeutos, while Amyraut's more meditative Exercitatio retreats to bare scriptural usage - only the Son is "begotten," only the Spirit "proceeds" - with real apophatic reserve about the mechanism itself [amyraut-exercitatio-symbolum-apostolorum/p249]. Calov notes patristic usage was looser, sometimes naming the Son's own generation a processio too [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-3/p576], against this later, harder antithesis; Abelard's earlier power/wisdom/goodness appropriation stands outside the apparatus entirely.

loci.label: Providence
loci.ov: In this corpus the providentia question is not whether God governs the world — settled already at Aquinas's own q.22 — but its de auxiliis extension: how infallible knowledge and efficacious concurrence over future free, contingent acts can consist with created liberty. Jesuits carry the greatest weight here — Suárez (the topic's most-represented author), Diego Ruiz de Montoya, and Molina himself hold that God knows futures through a scientia media logically prior to any decree of his will [molina-concordia-liberi-arbitrii-vol-1/p383], concursus fitted to each nature, freedom intact. Against them, the Dominican tradition on that same question (Soto-Zumel, the Salamanticenses, Poinsot, Billuart) locates that knowledge instead in a decree "determining" futurition, not a middle science [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-1/p454]. Scotists (Frassen) run a different three-state metaphysics — possibility, futurition, existence — where only futurition answers to any decree [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-2/p62]. Reformed scholastics (Zanchi, Daneau, Alting, Walaeus, Alsted) side structurally with the Dominicans, providence an eternal, all-determining consilium [zanchi-de-religione-christiana-fides/p333] — the alignment Calov attacks named Reformed (Chamier, Spanheim, Twisse, Maccovius) for conceding to "the Dominicans" [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-3/p1193], while Bechmann and Hülsemann keep providentia and praescientia a bare distinction of reason in their own Lutheran scheme.

loci.label: Subsistent Relations & the Divine Persons
loci.ov: This corpus's material on subsistent relations turns on one question: given one simple divine essence, what formally constitutes and distinguishes Father, Son, and Spirit as persons — relation itself, or some further subsistentia? The Thomist mainstream (Poinsot/John of St. Thomas, Salamanticenses, Soto/Zumel, Billuart) holds with Aquinas that "persona divina significat relationem ut subsistentem" [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-4-pt-1/p248], and that the distinguishing reality must be relative rather than absolute, since an absolute principle of distinction would divide the essence itself [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-4-pt-1/p177]. Scotus instead locates the constitutive relations of origin in a formal, not merely rational, non-identity with the simple infinite essence — a distinction he restricts to subsistents rather than creaturely "informants" [duns-scotus-opera-t10/p307]. Suárez, engaging Cajetan's reading of the Prima Pars, treats each personal subsistentia as itself a distinct perfection rather than a bare contraction of one absolute subsistence [suarez-opera-vol-17/p468]. The Scotist Juan de Rada's survey of rival opinions further opposes an absolute or common subsistence to Bonaventure's and Alexander of Hales's three properly relative subsistences, with no element common to all three [juan-de-rada-obs-controversiae-theologicae-inter-s-thomam-et-scotum-su-3/p67]. Reformed and Lutheran scholastics represented here (Alting, Gerhard, Martini) largely inherit this relation/essence apparatus rather than contest it.

loci.label: Religion / True Worship
loci.ov: In this corpus the treatise De Religione turns on two linked questions: what kind of virtue religio is, and what worship it licenses. Catholic scholastics converge on Aquinas's architecture: religio is the highest moral virtue, rendering cultus to God's excellentia, yet not itself a theological virtue, since it orders the acts of faith, hope and charity toward worship rather than terminating in God immediately -- Suarez argues this via Aquinas q.81 a.5 [suarez-opera-vol-18/p573]. Tournely extends the grid into apologetics for image-veneration: cultus divides into absolute (latria, owed to God and Christ alone) and relative, referred through an image to its prototype -- a refinement of Aquinas's own latria-dulia core, sharpened here for the era's controversies [tournely-praelectiones-theologicae-vol-4/p405]. Lutherans contest it on two fronts: Dannhauer works through the Jesuit Forer's claim that religio might be one virtue spanning latria and dulia [dannhauer-hodomoria/p1189], while Olearius makes true cultus whatever revelation alone institutes, necessarily one, owed to God solus [johann-olearius-universa-theologia/p37]. Forbes, writing Reformed historical theology, historicizes the vocabulary itself -- religio, cultus, latria, dulia, hyperdulia -- through Augustine [john-forbes-instructiones-historico-theologicae-vol-2/p316]. Suarez's own sprawling De Religione, plus Wirceburgensis, Bellarmine and Habert, anchor the Jesuit/Catholic bulk here; Voetius and Spanheim answer from the Reformed academies.

loci.label: Resurrection
loci.ov: Across this corpus 1 Corinthians 15:35–44, 53–54 sets the question: is the body raised the same body that died, altered in quality but not substance, or does new matter succeed the old? Lutheran (Gerhard, Calov, Meisner, Olearius, Bechmann) and Reformed (Braun, Alting, Beza, the Saumur Syntagma of Cappel, Amyraut, and La Place) authors converge against a shared target, Socinian denial of real bodily identity: the risen differ κατὰ τὰς ποιότητας, not κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν [calov-socinismus-profligatus/p1102]. Gerhard supplies the scholastic warrant — man is essentially soul-and-body, so identity of the man requires identity of the body's own matter, not the soul's alone, and the old puzzle of flesh consumed by beasts poses no real bar to reassembly [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-8/p1151]. The confessional seam runs less Lutheran/Reformed than orthodox/Socinian, though it surfaces obliquely where Beza insists Christ's own glorified flesh remains a defined, not repletive, presence, against the Lutheran ubiquitarian inference [beza-theses-theologicae-genevenses/p230]. Shared secondary loci: how dispersed matter is reassembled, likened to a householder's inventory [alting-scriptorum-theologicorum-heidelbergensium-vol-2/p243]; the dotes — incorruption, glory, power — replacing corruption, ignobility, infirmity [bechmann-annotationes-in-compendium-hutteri/p863]; and, in Sylvius's and Rada's Thomist-Scotist controversies, the hylomorphic conditions of identity itself.

loci.label: Sacraments
loci.ov: The locus turns on how, or whether, the sacraments themselves cause the grace they signify. The Catholic mainstream defines ex opere operato as true instrumental efficient causality: Tournely lists God's will, Christ's meritorious Passion, the minister's intention and power, and the rite's own external action as the causes concurring to justify, independent of the recipient's antecedent merit [tournely-praelectiones-theologicae-vol-6/p89]. The same causal schema recurs in the Scotist controversialist Juan de Rada, who, cataloguing disputes with Thomism, sorts the concurring causes into "moral" and "physical" modes [juan-de-rada-obs-controversiae-theologicae-inter-s-thomam-et-scotum-su-4/p58], a distinction internal to the Catholic schools. Reformed writers reject the analysis at its root: Vitringa juxtaposes Trent's own canons with Augustine and the Catholic canonist Pichler on opus operatum [vitringa-sr-observationes-sacrae-vol-6/p549], and Holzfuß, invoking Ames against Bellarmine, insists any sacramental instrumentality is moral, not physical, like bread nourishing a body [bartholomaus-holzfu-de-sacramentis/p51]. Lutherans hold a third line: Gerhard defends the sacraments as genuinely "exhibitive," not bare significations, against Beza and Aretius, while still binding their efficacy to faith [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-4/p460].

loci.label: Sanctification
loci.ov: Sanctification here turns less on a single disputed thesis than on where to place it among the applied benefits of grace, and how tightly to bind it to justification. Lutheran scholastics take sanctificatio (=renovatio) broadly, spanning vocation through justification, or strictly, as the act abolishing the "old man" — privation of powers, guilt, sin's dominion — and producing the "new," a habitual gift kept notionally distinct from the forensic act of justification even as its certain fruit [david-hollaz-examen-theologicum-acroamaticum/p977] [baier-compendium-theologiae-positivae-vol-3a/p300]. Olearius catalogues its many biblical names (mortification, crucifixion of the old man) while denying, against Huber's universalism, that God's universal intention yields universal actual holiness [johann-olearius-universa-theologia/p831]. Reformed federal theology draws the line more loosely: Maresius has regeneration "coincide with the gift of faith" itself, distinguishing only God's initiating act from the believer's own response [samuel-maresius-desmarets-systema-theologicum-cum-annotationibus-groni/p680], while Coccejus ties Hebrews 12:14 ("without sanctification no one shall see the Lord") to the claim that holiness is itself "the beginning of eternal life" [coccejus-summa-theologiae/p1257]. Suárez's Opera and the anti-Tridentine Chamier and Heidegger volumes mark the unstated third position: habitual grace as justification's formal cause, not its consequence.

loci.label: God's Knowledge & Middle Knowledge
loci.ov: In this corpus the sub-locus descends from the medieval Sentences-commentary treatment of God's foreknowledge of future contingents (so Bonaventure, In Sent. I) and, after Molina's 1588 Concordia, sharpens into one technical dispute: is a conditioned future contingent — what a free creature would do under an unrealized supposition — known to God by a scientia media logically antecedent to any decree of the will, or only within the decree? Molina posits such a science, between scientia naturalis and scientia libera [molina-concordia-liberi-arbitrii-vol-1/p359]; Jesuits follow him. Thomists (Domingo de Soto/Zumel [domingo-de-soto-zumel-salamanca-commentary-vol-1/p415], Poinsot, Salamanticenses, Gonet, Billuart) deny any such object apart from a predetermining decree, tying the question to Báñezian physical premotion — Wirceburgensis records Thomists and Scotists requiring the decree against "almost all others" [wirceburgensis-theologia-wirceburgensis-vol-2/p118], and Billuart calls it the question dividing "the Fathers of the Society... and all other Theologians, especially Thomists" [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-1/p425]. Reformed scholastics (Rutherford, invoking the Tyre/Keilah/Ezekiel counterfactuals [rutherford-examen-arminianismi/p217], with Voetius, Strangius, Twisse, Crocius, Burgersdijck) reject scientia media outright, folding the disputed cases back into scientia simplicis intelligentiae under the decree.

loci.label: Scripture
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus de scriptura turns on two linked questions: is Scripture alone a "perfect," self-sufficient rule of faith, and who adjudicates when its sense is disputed? Gerhard supplies the base distinction Lutheran orthodoxy repeats: Scripture as the "absolute" judge, the Spirit's own voice, versus the church's merely "ministerial" judgment [gerhard-confessio-catholica-liber-1/p142]. Fabricius restates this almost verbatim, citing Gerhard by name [johann-fabricius-consideratio-controversiarum/p12], while Quenstedt turns Scripture's "perfection" against Catholic controversialists like Tanner, rejecting their regula totalis/partialis — Scripture as a partial rule needing tradition's completion [quenstedt-systema-theologicum/p113], the position Suárez and the Walenburg brothers occupy from the Roman side. Reformed writers reach the same conclusion by a different route, perspicuity and self-interpretation rather than Gerhard's judge-apparatus: Pareus's 1605 Heidelberg disputation makes Scripture sui ipsius interpres against pope, council, or prince [pareus-collegia-theologica/p581], and Strangius devotes a monograph to its perfection from Ps. 19:7, alongside Chamier's vast anti-Roman Panstratia. Later orthodoxy (Hollaz) formalizes a technical pair — articles held ῥητῶς αὐτολεξεὶ, explicitly, versus those held only διανοητικῶς κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα, by necessary consequence [david-hollaz-examen-theologicum-acroamaticum/p203] — sharpening, not originating, the older distinction.

loci.label: Divine Simplicity
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns on whether the divine essence's exclusion of composition — physical (matter/form, integral parts) and metaphysical (genus/differentia, essence/existence, act/potency, subject/accident) — leaves room for plural attributes and three Trinitarian persons, and if so what grade of distinction underlies them: real, formal, or rational. The consensus floor admits no real distinction: Gerhard calls goodness, power and wisdom "realiter unum" with the essence, named attributes rather than accidents since nothing is added to it [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1/p253]; Calov likewise strips out essence/subsistence composition as yielding a "quaternitas" in the Trinity [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-2/p304]. Reformed and Lutheran authors — and, on Frassen's report, the Thomist bench (Salamanticenses, Poinsot, Soto/Zumel) — locate any remaining difference in a distinction of reason grounded in God's relations to creatures, not a parte rei: for Leydekker it arises "in our very feeble intellect" [leydekker-de-veritate-religionis-reformatae/p14]. Habert instead worries the distinction can collapse too far, into the merely nominal identity of Eunomius, Aetius, and the Nominalists — Ockham's school elsewhere here [habert-theologia-dogmatica-moralis-vol-1/p253]. Scotists (Frassen, Mastri) press a stronger formal distinction a parte rei, arguing ad hominem from the Trinity: persons differ really from each other yet only rationally from the essence, so distinction-free simplicity was never God's condition [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p262].

loci.label: The Holy Spirit
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus regularly splits into two questions inherited from the patristic-conciliar deposit: the Spirit's full consubstantial deity, defended against the ancient Macedonians and Pneumatomachi; and the more contested early-modern question of whether he proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle (Filioque) or from the Father alone [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1/p661; simmler-de-aeterno-dei-filio/p721]. Structurally the second question descends from Lombard's Sentences I, dist. 10-13, the terrain of this corpus's Sentences-commentators (Bonaventure, Estius, Soto-Zumel, Daneau) and its dedicated Trinity treatises (Zamora, Aguirre, Suarez). On the Filioque itself, Catholic (Habert, reconciling Damascene's "through the Son" via Aquinas) [habert-theologia-dogmatica-moralis-vol-1/p657], Lutheran (Calov, arguing Father and Son are "one and the same breathing," one principle not two) [calov-systema-locorum-theologicorum-vol-3/p844], and Reformed (Amyraut, weighing the Greek ekporeuesthai with real exegetical care before declining its exclusive sense) [amyraut-de-mysterio-trinitatis/p389] positions converge. The line that actually divides opinion in these sources runs West against Greek East, not Catholic against Protestant.

loci.label: The Trinity
loci.ov: In this corpus the treatise on the Trinity is worked less as a Protestant-Catholic battleground than as a shared scholastic-Augustinian grammar, defended in common against Socinian and "Greek" dissent, with the real school lines falling within the West rather than across it. The recurring question is how two immanent processions — generation per modum intellectus, spiration per modum voluntatis, a distinction Reformed scholastics themselves trace to "the Scholastics, in primis Thoma" and to Lombard [daneau-christianae-isagoges/p78] — ground really distinct subsistent relations in one numerically simple essence. Thomist commentary works out the Spirit's single "spirative principle" in Father-and-Son as one relation, not two [de-potentia-dei-cum-commentariis/p984]; the Scotist Frassen argues the same two-processions thesis from Scripture and the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Lateran, and Florence [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-3/p88]. The Filioque itself is defended against the Greeks by Reformed authors (Amyraut, who still judges the Latins "more severe" than the point requires [amyraut-de-mysterio-trinitatis/p404]) and Lutherans (Gerhard [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-1/p678]) alike. Ruiz de Montoya, Suárez, Petavius, Zamora, Aguirre, Wirceburgensis, and Reding among Catholics, and Quenstedt, Melanchthon, and Carpzov among Lutherans, all work the same relations-and-processions apparatus toward a shared anti-Socinian conclusion: three really distinct, coequal, coeternal persons in one simple essence.

loci.label: Virtues / Moral Theology
loci.ov: The locus turns on whether grace produces really distinct infused habits of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance over and above the naturally acquired virtues, and, correlatively, whether prudence and moral virtue necessarily entail each other (connexio virtutum). The Thomist cursus-writers (Salamanticenses, Poinsot) make prudence the single habit uniting all the moral virtues' matter [salamanticenses-cursus-theologicus-vol-6/p398]. The Coimbra Jesuits side with Aquinas, Cajetan, and Capreolus that some moral virtues are given per se infused, since supernatural beatitude requires a different mean than the naturally acquired virtues supply [collegium-conimbricense-in-libros-ethicorum/p77]; Suárez affirms the correlative claim that perfect prudence cannot be acquired without the moral virtues, calling this the "mens Aristotelis et D. Thomae" [suarez-opera-vol-4/p521]. Scotus complicates the entailment by asking whether prudence, as an intellectual habit dictating end or means, could be preserved without the will's corresponding right election [duns-scotus-opera-t15/p669] — a move later worked by the properly Scotist Mastri and, on the separate Bonaventurian line, by Barberi's Cursus "ad mentem S. Bonaventurae," both building on Bonaventure and William of Auxerre's pre-split thirteenth-century synthesis. Reformed dogmatics (Wendelin) imports the Thomist apparatus directly rather than staking a confessional alternative [wendelin-christianae-theologiae-libri-ii/p849]; the operative fault line here runs school, not confession.

loci.label: Eternal Life
loci.ov: Across this corpus vita aeterna is defined fairly uniformly as fruition or vision of God—Daneau's formula is simply "visio gloriosa Dei" [daneau-isagoges-christianae-pars-quarta/p649]—while Alsted, surveying Augustine and Bernard on the term, dismisses the scholastic substantial/accidental-reward distinction as an inept "Sorbonist" refinement rather than part of that inherited definition [alsted-theologia-scholastica-didactica/p871]. The live dispute is whether this life falls under meritum de condigno. Thomists hold that only grace, itself "aequalis valoris cum visione beatifica," can ground condign merit, as the Salamanticenses argue [salamanticenses-cursus-theologicus-vol-10/p728], and Jesuits (Bellarmine, Molina, Ripalda, Becanus) press the same case: Bellarmine reads the vineyard denarius as a iustum pretium for labor [bellarmine-disputationes-de-controversiis-vol-3-as/p667]. Lutherans (Gerhard, Calov, Bechmann, Quenstedt, Carpzov) and Reformed (Pareus, Bucanus, Coccejus) deny it outright as a bare gratuitous gift; Gerhard rereads the identical denarius parable, against Bellarmine's own distinction, to prove equality rather than proportion, invoking Prosper against any work-reward even under grace [gerhard-loci-theologici-tomus-4/p259]. Scotists (Frassen, Mastri), also prominent in this locus, hold the same Catholic line.

loci.label: The Will of God
loci.ov: In this corpus the locus turns less on whether God wills than on the taxonomy needed to say so without compromising divine simplicity or making God the author of sin: voluntas signi versus beneplaciti, and within beneplacitum, antecedens versus consequens, efficax versus inefficax. Billuart traces the antecedent/consequent pair to Chrysostom and Damascene before Aquinas, noting that although every theologian uses it, "non omnes tamen eam uno modo explicant" [billuart-summa-s-thomae-vol-2/p42]; Alsted's aphorisms show the full Reformed-scholastic uptake of the same grid [alsted-theologia-scholastica-didactica/p526]. Pressure concentrates on sin: Strangius's treatise on God's will and actions concerning sin fixes beneplacitum's broader sense (embracing inefficacious antecedent willing) against the stricter sense most prefer, efficacious willing alone [strangius-de-voluntate-et-actionibus-dei-circa-peccatum/p45], while Braun rebuts the Lutheran charge that distinguishing decretive from preceptive will posits "voluntates contrarias" in God [braun-doctrina-foederum/p108]. Poinsot's Thomist Cursus identifies efficacious will strictly with the consequent, executed through every requisite circumstance [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-8/p98] — the premotion-leaning construal that Suárez's congruism (four Opera volumes among the most-engaged works here) contests from within Catholic scholasticism, while Twisse mounts an analogous anti-Molinist case from the Reformed side.

loci.label: Prolegomena / Theological Method
loci.ov: In this corpus, prolegomena keeps returning to one question: does theology satisfy Aristotle's definition of scientia — certain knowledge demonstrated from evident principles — or is it a habitus of another kind? The line runs through the scholastic schools more than across confessions. Thomists (Poinsot, Reding, Gonet, Billuart) answer yes, but only as a subalternated science, resolving not into principles evident in themselves but into the science proper to God and the blessed, communicated through faith [poinsot-john-of-st-thomas-cursus-theologicus-vol-1/p453]. Scotist Frassen agrees on the label but argues it from the Fathers, chiefly Augustine, rather than subalternation [frassen-scotus-academicus-vol-1/p96]; Ockham denies it outright, since no believer's grasp of the credibilia is more evident than an old woman's [william-of-ockham-william-of-ockham-scriptum-in-libros-sententiarum/p44]. Jesuit Petavius keeps the name but relocates theology's principles in authority and faith, not demonstration [petavius-de-theologicis-dogmatibus-vol-1/p89]. The same question opens Voetius's and Junius's Reformed prolegomena; Maccovius pushes it toward the practical, denying theology is a contemplative science and calling it instead a habitus tending to godliness [maccovius-loci-communes-collegia-theologica-vol-2/p20].
